title: TRAE official homepage
raw_excerpt: TRAE homepage positions the product around shipping faster and says TRAE SOLO lets the user define the task, review results, and let AI handle the rest. Useful for product positioning and top-level value proposition.

title: What is Trae Builder?
raw_excerpt: Trae Builder is documented as a mode for developing a complete project from scratch. It actively reads current project files, breaks down tasks, creates or edits files, generates and runs commands, analyzes command execution, supports code-change preview, accept/reject flows, webview preview, and reversion within the latest Builder window.

title: SOLO: The Responsive Coding Agent
raw_excerpt: TRAE SOLO is positioned as a responsive coding agent and visual workspace. The page says TRAE IDE was built for AI-first coding with deep contextual understanding, conversational interaction, and multi-agent collaboration. SOLO works across IDE, terminal, DocView, browser, connector, Figma, requirements, prototyping, frontend, backend, debugging, optimization, build and deployment. It also emphasizes parallel agents, structured plans, TODO lists, review visibility, and real-time context.

title: The Register: Trae AI IDE telemetry continues even after opt-out, report says
raw_excerpt: The Register reported allegations that Trae produced extensive network activity even when telemetry was disabled, including system information, usage patterns, performance metrics, machine identifiers, user ID, and project information. The article also notes ByteDance's later clarification that the IDE telemetry toggle only controlled telemetry through the VS Code IDE framework, while other Trae tools were unaffected. Treat as third-party risk signal, not official product claim.

title: Cursor official product page
raw_excerpt: Cursor positions itself as a coding agent built to make developers extraordinarily productive. The page emphasizes agents that turn ideas into code, autonomous end-to-end build/test/demo workflows, parallel work, CLI, Slack, GitHub PR review, model choice across OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/xAI/Cursor, codebase understanding, secure codebase indexing, and enterprise adoption.

title: Cursor Background Agents documentation
raw_excerpt: Cursor Background Agents are asynchronous remote agents that edit and run code in a remote Ubuntu-based environment. They can clone GitHub repositories, work on a separate branch, install packages, run commands, receive follow-ups, and push changes for handoff. The docs also flag security considerations: internet access, auto-running terminal commands, data retention for a few days, and prompt-injection/exfiltration risk.

title: Cursor pricing documentation
raw_excerpt: Cursor pricing docs describe agent usage as model-inference/API-cost based. Pro includes a pool of agent API usage plus bonus usage; Teams is listed at $40 per user per month with pooled usage and admin controls. Background Agent pricing is tied to selected model API costs. Privacy Mode can be enforced in team contexts, while remote features may require temporary code retention for operation.

title: Windsurf Cascade documentation
raw_excerpt: Windsurf Cascade is documented as an agentic AI assistant with Code and Chat modes, tool calling, voice input, checkpoints, real-time awareness, linter integration, web search, memories/rules, MCP, terminal, workflows and app deploys. It has built-in planning through todo lists, can queue messages, call tools, create named checkpoints, revert changes, and run multiple Cascades simultaneously, with race-risk if two Cascades edit the same file.

title: Windsurf model availability documentation
raw_excerpt: Windsurf documentation lists available models for Cascade, including Windsurf SWE models and external Claude/GPT-style options depending on plan and availability. The model-selector model matters for product analysis because AI coding IDE quality depends on both the orchestration shell and model access policy.

title: Windsurf plans and usage documentation
raw_excerpt: Windsurf's account documentation explains plan and usage tracking across Free, Pro, Teams and Enterprise. Search results and docs indicate token/model usage and quota management have become central to the pricing experience, with extra usage purchase paths for paid plans. Use this for business model and pricing-risk analysis rather than exact plan arithmetic.

title: GitHub Copilot cloud agent docs
raw_excerpt: GitHub Copilot cloud agent is documented as an autonomous agent in the GitHub workflow. Users can assign it tasks from issues or connected tools; it works through planning, code changes, tests, pull requests and review handoff inside GitHub's governance surface. Important for enterprise positioning because GitHub owns repository, PR, Actions and security workflows.

title: GitHub Copilot agents product page
raw_excerpt: GitHub says Copilot can be assigned from GitHub Issues, Azure Boards, Jira, Raycast, Linear, IDEs and CLI. The page emphasizes that planning context travels with the task and Copilot can be routed from Slack or Teams. This makes Copilot more of a workflow-native teammate than only an IDE plugin.

title: GitHub Copilot plans
raw_excerpt: GitHub Copilot plan documentation lists Free, Student, Pro, Pro+, Business and Enterprise variants. The docs describe unlimited completions for paid tiers, premium models in Copilot Chat, cloud agent access, monthly premium request allowances, organization policy control, and enterprise-grade management. New self-serve signups were temporarily paused in April 2026 for several plans.

title: GitHub Copilot requests and billing
raw_excerpt: GitHub docs state that starting June 1, 2026 Copilot is moving from request-based billing to usage-based billing. The same page says agentic features consume premium requests based on prompts/sessions and model rates, while cloud-agent sessions and steering comments have dedicated metering. This is a strong signal that autonomous coding workloads are too expensive for simple flat pricing.

title: Claude Code overview
raw_excerpt: Claude Code is documented as an agentic coding tool that reads the codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with terminal, IDE, desktop app and browser. It helps build features, fix bugs, automate development tasks, work across multiple files/tools, stage changes, write commit messages, create branches and open pull requests.

title: Claude Code models, usage and limits
raw_excerpt: Anthropic help docs explain Claude Code usage metering by Enterprise seat pool or API key pay-as-you-go. The model guidance suggests Sonnet for most coding, Opus for hard debugging or architectural work, and Haiku for cheap simple edits. It highlights that long sessions grow context/cost and recommends /clear and /compact to manage usage.

title: Claude Code data usage
raw_excerpt: Claude Code data-usage documentation distinguishes consumer, commercial, API and third-party platform handling. Commercial terms and enterprise deployment matter for teams evaluating whether code and prompts can be used for model improvement, how retention works, and what policies apply to development data.

title: OpenAI: Introducing the Codex app
raw_excerpt: OpenAI introduced the Codex desktop app as a command center for agents. The article says developers now orchestrate multiple agents across projects, delegate work, run tasks in parallel, and supervise substantial work that can span hours, days or weeks. The app supports separate threads, diff review, comments, editor handoff, and worktrees so multiple agents can work on the same repository without conflicts.

title: OpenAI Codex app skills, automations and sandboxing
raw_excerpt: OpenAI says Codex is evolving from writing code into using code to get work done. The Codex app supports skills, automations, personality modes, review queues, native/open-source sandboxing, folder/branch limits, cached web search, permission prompts for elevated actions, and configurable team rules. This source is useful for architecture and trust/safety comparison.

title: OpenAI Help Center: Codex rate card
raw_excerpt: OpenAI Help Center says Codex pricing was updated in April 2026 to align with API token usage rather than per-message pricing. The rate card maps credits to input, cached input and output tokens and notes that average Codex cost is roughly $100-$200 per developer per month with large variance depending on model choice, number of instances, automations and fast mode.

title: Devin enterprise deployment documentation
raw_excerpt: Devin documentation says Devin can be initiated through web interface, Slack or API and operates in a workspace with shell, browser and code editor. Its architecture separates a cloud-based Brain from a Devbox execution environment. Enterprise deployment choices include multi-tenant cloud and customer-dedicated single-tenant environments with PrivateLink/IPSec options for private resources.

title: Cognition: New self-serve plans for Devin
raw_excerpt: Cognition announced new Devin self-serve pricing in April 2026: Free, Pro at $20/month, Max at $200/month, Teams usage-based with $80/month minimum spend, and Enterprise custom pricing. The post says old Core and Team plans are retired, products like Ask Devin, DeepWiki and Devin Review begin charging, and pricing should reflect compute-heavy work while giving users better controls and cost guidance.

title: Devin 2026 release notes
raw_excerpt: Devin 2026 release notes include enterprise controls such as default platform settings, session categorization, usage breakdowns, guardrails, MCP marketplace upgrades, audit logs, session ACU caps, review consumption by repository, and higher-quality Wiki v2 using stronger reasoning and subagents. These show Devin's focus on enterprise agent operations, governance and cost visibility.

title: Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey for Leaders: AI adoption and trust
raw_excerpt: Stack Overflow reports that 84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools in 2025, up from 76% in 2024, while trust declined: only 29% said they trust AI outputs to be accurate and more developers actively distrust accuracy than trust it. This supports a market insight: adoption is no longer the bottleneck; trust, verification and workflow integration are.

title: Stack Overflow blog: Closing the developer AI trust gap
raw_excerpt: Stack Overflow defines developer trust as willingness to deploy AI-generated code to production with minimal review and confidence that tools will not introduce unacceptable risks or technical debt. This source helps shape the user analysis: AI coding agents must earn trust through reviewability, grounding, test execution, rollback and governance.

title: arXiv: Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents on GitHub
raw_excerpt: The paper studies coding-agent traces across 128,018 GitHub projects and estimates adoption of coding agents at 22.20%-28.66%, high for a new tool category. It frames agents such as Cursor, Claude Code and Codex as different from traditional code-completion tools because they can generate complete pull requests from task descriptions.
